source.title: Investigating Professional Money Laundering, Underground Banking, and the Use of Hawala and Other Similar Service Providers

summary: GOLDEN LABEL, hand-drafted against the PDF. FATF typologies report, from a 46-jurisdiction survey, on how professional money launderers misuse hawala, underground banking and similar providers. Its central finding is an updated five-way typology of how operators settle net balances: bilateral offsetting, triangular or network settlement through third jurisdictions, settlement through value (cash couriers, over- and under-invoicing, phantom trade, gold and luxury goods, BMPE-style three-way exchange), formal-channel settlement via shell companies, mules, structured deposits, cuckoo smurfing and crowdfunding narratives, and digital settlement in stablecoins. Global trends are digitalisation (encrypted messaging, hawala apps, AI-driven routing), professionalisation with enablers, and deep integration with banks, PSPs, vIBANs, prepaid cards and mobile money; regional patterns cover mobile-money hawala in Africa and Asia, VA-plus-gold hybrids in the Middle East, BMPE in Latin America, Chinese-speaking laundering networks and emerging settlement hubs in Asia and the Middle East. Sections 2 and 3 cover challenges and good practice and carry no new typologies beyond the case boxes.

while traders benefited from off-book payments and the undervaluation of imported goods.
In trade- based settlement schemes, underground bankers or HOSSPs use import–export front companies to manipulate invoices—through over- or under-invoicing and falsified cargo descriptions
Use of import/export fronts and wholesale trading structures to balance accounts through over - or under-invoicing, falsified cargo descriptions and commercial offsets;

False invoices for goods such as pharmaceuticals and clothing were used to simulate legitimate purchases, although no goods were delivered.

The settlement model evolved from courier -based cash smuggling to non -physical mechanisms, including fictitious t rade transactions, multi -jurisdictional financial triangulation, and internal offsetting.

Goods were exported to related entities in a third jurisdiction, where payment was deliberately withheld on the basis of fictitious commercial disputes, before the goods were re-exported to entities controlled by the same network.
A related manifestation involves clearing via third -party transfers i.e. the settlement of balances through unconnected third parties
a distinction exists between third-party payments—where the exporter is paid by an entity other than the invoiced customer, often controlled by the PML network—and TBML itself
In March 2022, Indian authorities identified a transnational PML scheme that used shell companies and trade transactions to transfer value across jurisdictions.
The companies were incorporated through nominees, often using stolen or forged Know your customer  (KYC) documents, and had limited or no genuine business activity.
Third party money mules are commonly used to fragment large-sum criminal cash into multiple small deposits and transfer them to designated accounts, avoiding the AML monitoring thresholds of FIs.
Money mule networks, including students or temporary residents abroad, used to fragment deposits and reduce suspicion;
Mule accounts, including accounts held by young persons or migrants, are used across banks, payment institutions, and VASPs to receive and move funds.
The schemes were supported by mule accounts, accounts held in false or third -party names, unregistered VA exchange activity
Multiple ‘alias accounts’  may route incoming payments to a central master account, creating a nesting effect and shielding illicit activity behind regulated intermediation.
Corporate vehicles and cover accounts were also used to channel funds through the banking system, often showing many- to-one transfers and cash activity inconsistent with the stated customer profile.
this threshold -triggered “sweeping” helps move funds rapidly through multiple accounts, reducing the time proceeds remain in any single account and limiting manual intervention by operators.

Professional money launderers leverage these characteristics to consolid ate, convert, and move illicit proceeds rapidly, facilitating swift layering and distribution while bypassing regulated channels.
jurisdictions report that underground banking systems and HOSSPs operate ancillary businesses, most commonly import/export and trading companies, followed by professional service firms
Cash- intensive businesses, such as kiosks, hookah bars, mobile phone shops or souvenir shops, provided cover for cash deposits, third-party payments, and mixed funding sources.
Criminal cash was collected through front businesses in the import -export sector, particularly clothing and fashion, which acted as covert cash collection hubs despite limited genuine activity.

Settlement may be disguised as legitimate commercial activity and facilitated through shell companies, money-mule accounts, virtual IBANs (vIBANs), or corporate structures. Wire transfers, batch payments, and layered transactions are common features.
More complex layering: Digital tools enable rapid combination of multiple channels (PSPs, VAs, mule accounts, trade), increasing transaction complexity and hindering reconstruction.
Criminals may deploy terminals through complicit or fictitious businesses to process sham transactions, introducing illicit funds into regulated systems under the guise of legitimate revenue.

Professional money launderers typically establish and maintain enduring ML infrastructure, including shell companies and other legal persons or arrangements, and rely on facilitators and multiple layers of intermediaries
rapid freezing, seizure, and potential confiscation of funds held by short -lived shell companies suspected of being used for ML
criminal cash was introduced into the financial system through business bank accounts linked to shell or sham companies, often controlled by nominees.
Networks often maintain multiple bank accounts, including those held by nominees or shell entities, and use tools such as vIBANs to facilitate rapid cross-border transfers.

typologies.label: Hawala net settlement by compensation between counterpart operators

citations.quote: Instead, counterpart operators in different jurisdict ions settle obligations through internal book -entries and subsequent compensation, which may involve trade transactions, cash pooling, or alternative asset movements.
In its most basic form, settlement occurs through direct, bilateral offsetting of obligations between two service providers.

typologies.label: Triangular or multi-node settlement through third jurisdictions

citations.quote: A core method in contemporary underground banking and HOSSPs involves multilateral compensation across a network of brokers , in which balances between HOSSPs are settled indirectly through third jurisdictions.

typologies.label: Cash-courier and bulk-cash settlement between service providers

citations.quote: Cash couriers, namely individuals who physically transport cash or bearer negotiable instruments on behalf of others, often across borders, to rebalance positions between service providers;
One scheme involved couriers transporting over GBP 130 million  (approximately USD 171 million) in cash to the UAE over a three-month period.

typologies.label: Commodity and gold-backed settlement, including luxury-goods repurchase

citations.quote: gold functions both as a reserve asset underpinning VA settlement balances and as a physical medium used to reconcile outstanding obligations between HOSSPs
Daigou-style luxury -goods repurchase networks, whereby criminal cash is converted into high-value goods purchased in Europe and resold in Asia;
Nigerian funds were transferred to gold traders, who co-ordinated with counterparts in the United Kingdom to deliver equivalent cash to a nominee.

typologies.label: Virtual-asset and stablecoin settlement between underground banking operators

citations.quote: Increasingly, obligations between HOSSPs are settled using digital value -transfer mechanisms , including VAs (particularly stablecoins to reduce price volatility), online PSPs, and digital banking platforms.
VA transfers were used to compensate the cash -providing branch, allowing the network to balance obligations without direct bank transfers.

typologies.label: Cuckoo smurfing through unwitting legitimate remitters

citations.quote: ‘cuckoo smurfing’ , a form of third -party payment whereby illicit cash is deposited into the bank account of an unsuspecting legitimate remitter. The remitter’s genuine outbound transfer is then used to settle obligations offshore

typologies.label: Black market peso exchange and three-way exchange exploiting capital controls

citations.quote: Three-way exchange and mirror -transaction models, in which illicit funds generated in one jurisdiction are exchanged for local funds from individuals seeking to transfer value overseas (e.g. to circumvent capital controls).
BMPE mirrors underground banking and HOSSP systems by transferring value across borders without the physical movement of funds, relying instead on commercial trade flows to settle obligations.
Three-way exchange in which cartel- generated US dollars are sold to individuals seeking to circumvent capital controls.

typologies.label: Digital hawala: encrypted-messaging co-ordination, hawala apps and AI-driven routing

citations.quote: “Digital hawala” broadly refers to the use of digital technologies to facilitate the co-ordination, execution, settlement, or concealment of informal value transfer.
Some jurisdictions report the use of AI -based tools to facilitate PML, including automated structuring of transactions, dynamic routing across mule accounts and payment platforms

typologies.label: Mobile-money integration with hawala for cash-in and cash-out

citations.quote: In most cases, mobile money is used by customers to cash in and cash out funds to and from underground banking operators and HOSSPs, with end users experiencing near -instant transfers through mobile wallets.
The hawaladars then sent screenshots evidencing payment through an e -wallet to a corresponding e -wallet maintained with a payment service provider in Jurisdiction A.
HOSSPs remain a core TF method, particularly in high-risk contexts.
Türkiye identified a ‘digital hawala’ network used to finance members of the terrorist organisation Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant (ISIL).

actors.name: Professional money launderers
actors.role: Third-party launderers selling ML services to criminals for a fee or commission; the threat the report is about

citations.quote: refers to individuals, organisations or networks providing ML services to criminals in exchange for a commission, fee, or other profit.

actors.name: Hawaladars and underground bankers
actors.role: Network brokers controlling cash pools and ledgers, usually behind legitimate ancillary businesses

citations.quote: Underground bankers/Hawaladars : Network brokers controlling cash pools and ledgers, frequently operating from legitimate ancillary businesses (e.g., travel agencies, money exchange shops, import/export firms, wholesalers).

actors.name: Controllers and international controller networks
actors.role: Trusted individuals who arrange collection of criminal proceeds and delivery of equivalent value, co-ordinating brokers, collectors and transmitters across jurisdictions

citations.quote: controllers—also referred to in some jurisdictions as ‘money brokers’ or ‘superfacilitators’—are trusted individuals who arrange the collection of criminal proceeds and the delivery of equivalent value to the intended destination.

actors.name: Cash couriers
actors.role: Individuals physically transporting cash or bearer instruments across borders to rebalance positions between service providers

citations.quote: Individual who physically transports cash or bearer negotiable instruments on behalf of others, often across borders, to rebalance positions between service providers.

actors.name: Money mules
actors.role: Persons moving criminal proceeds through their own accounts to fragment deposits and settle balances via formal channels

citations.quote: Person who transfers, moves, deposits, withdraws, or converts criminal proceeds on behalf of another person or criminal network, typically through their own financial accounts

actors.name: Chinese-speaking money laundering networks
actors.role: High-capacity transnational PML networks with operational links to East Asia, running cash consolidation hubs and displacing BMPE brokers

citations.quote: Jurisdictions also identify a distinct and growing pattern involving PML networks with operational links to East Asia, including money launderers in these jurisdictions, facilitators based in the region and/or abroad
Italian authorities have identified cases involving Chinese underground banking networks, where illicit proc eeds were transferred abroad through non -EU PSPs

actors.name: Professional enablers
actors.role: Lawyers, accountants, notaries, corporate formation agents and similar professionals facilitating PML schemes, knowingly or through wilful blindness

citations.quote: Jurisdictions also report increasing involvement of professional service providers—including lawyers, accountants, auditors, notaries, corporate formation agents, financial consultants, real estate agents

Professional money launderers are diverse and often include legal professionals (such as lawyers and notaries), financial intermediaries (including accountants and financial advisers), and individuals operating informal networks.

actors.name: Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant
actors.role: Terrorist organisation financed through a digital hawala network in Türkiye using jeweller and mobile-phone-shop fronts

citations.quote: A jeweller and two mobile phone shops were identified as fronts for hawala transactions.

actors.name: Transnational organised crime groups
actors.role: Primary clients of hawala-based PML, chiefly drug traffickers

citations.quote: Across multiple jurisdictions, transnational organised crime groups remain the primary users of underground banking and HOSSPs for PML.

extraction_notes: Golden label. Printed folio is PDF page minus 2 for pages 3-75. VA settlement is NOT labelled CMI010: the library entry is sanctions-scoped and the report frames VAs as PML settlement, so it is emergent under crypto. Front companies are not SAN004 (sanctions-scoped); they are labelled BA007 and TBML009. TBML001 kept at medium: over-invoicing is named in the settlement typology (p25, p41) but every worked case is under-invoicing. TBML005 false cargo descriptions, crowdfunding-as-settlement (Box 4), banknote-serial tokens and prepaid-card bridging are mentioned but not labelled (indicators or single boxes). vIBAN nesting is cited under BA002 rather than as its own emergent. Chinese-speaking networks carry no jurisdiction: the report calls them a linguistic/diaspora category with East Asia links. Operation names (Klaver, Karasu, Whitewall, Fei Ch'ien, Cymbal) and Box 29 panel operators are anonymised, not actors. Jurisdictions are case and hub locations; survey respondents and good-practice states (SE, FR, BD, LU, MY, CH, PT, ID, KE) are excluded. REVIEWED 2026-09-11. Added TBML005 False Description Of Goods at medium: 'falsified cargo descriptions' is named twice, both times inside the report's own enumerations of trade-based settlement techniques. TBML006's citation was extended: it stopped at 'payment was deliberately withheld', which does not close a circle; the sentence continues 'before the goods were re-exported to entities controlled by the same network', and the paragraph opens by naming 'circular trade flows' outright. PAT009 Related Party Trading was considered on that same sentence and left out: the related-entity trade is the vehicle for the circular flow the report names as the technique, and PAT009 is nowhere described as a technique in its own right in a 76-page narrative. BA007 is correct here on p27's kiosks, hookah bars and mobile phone shops -- the fourth document in this set to settle that mapping on its evidence.
